title: Bangladesh garment protests spread to more highways as 264 factories shut near Dhaka
dek: Workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway and the Dhaka-Narayanganj link road on Monday, the third day of unrest over pay, as the home minister ordered a crackdown on violence and blamed owners linked to the Awami League.

body:
Bangladesh's garment wage protests spread on Monday, the third day of unrest, as thousands of workers blocked highways and clashed with police around Dhaka. Hundreds of workers in Gazipur blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway and vandalised several vehicles, while police fired tear gas to disperse large crowds in the capital's Mirpur district, AFP reported. Workers also blocked the Dhaka-Narayanganj link road for about five hours, and two pickup vans were set on fire in Gazipur, The Daily Star reported. It said 264 factories in Ashulia and Savar, on Dhaka's outskirts, were shut.

Workers want the monthly minimum wage raised to Tk 30,000 from Tk 12,500. The government formed a new six-member wage board on Sunday, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman held an emergency meeting with senior ministers that evening, but the move "failed to immediately quell unrest", Reuters said. Kamrul Hasan, general secretary of the Ekota Garments Sramik Federation, told AFP that some labour leaders had gone into hiding, and that unions had not been prepared for the unrest "as the wage board has already been formed".

## Tuesday: fourth day

Garment workers staged a fourth day of wage protests on Tuesday, with police firing tear gas to disperse demonstrators, Reuters reported from Dhaka. The unrest, which began on Saturday, has intensified despite the government's formation of a six-member wage board on 1 November. Clashes were reported in Ashulia, Gazipur and Dhaka's Mirpur area, where workers tried to block major highways, and Reuters said dozens of people, including several police officers, were injured. In Ashulia, police fired tear gas and sound grenades after protesters threw bricks and stones, said Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of Ashulia Industrial Police. Several factories in Gazipur and Ashulia again suspended operations or declared holidays after nearly 700 had stopped work the previous day, Reuters said. Daily Waadaa put the number shut on Tuesday at around 500; the counts differ by source and are approximate.

Reuters noted that factory owners cite rising operating costs, uncertainty in energy markets linked to the Middle East conflict and softer demand, and warn that prolonged unrest could jeopardise spring and summer export orders. The sector employs about 4 million workers, supplies brands such as H&M, Zara and Gap, and accounts for more than 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings. Workers want Tk 30,000 a month (about $245) against the current Tk 12,500.

## Home minister's warning

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the prime minister had instructed the government "to ensure that production and exports continue unhindered", and that law enforcement agencies were being asked to crack down on those involved in violence, AFP reported. The Daily Star reported that he blamed factory owners linked to the former Awami League government for fuelling the unrest; he did not name any owners and no evidence was made public. The Awami League, which is banned, had not responded. Worker representatives on Monday urged workers to return to work and called for the release of those detained, The Daily Star reported.

## Monday's clashes

In Dhaka, police used tear gas to disperse workers who were blocking roads after protesters threw bricks and stones, Reuters reported. In Ashulia, on the capital's outskirts, police fired tear gas and water cannon at workers trying to block a highway. Al Jazeera's correspondent reported a heavy police presence in Dhaka's Mirpur industrial area. No injury figures for Monday had been reported.

After meeting garment industry leaders on Monday, the home minister also warned that those "attempting to destabilise the country will be dealt with firmly", Reuters reported. Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury urged workers to go back to work, saying their demand for a wage board had been met, Business Standard reported, citing The Daily Star.

The president of the manufacturers' association BGMEA, Mahmud Hasan Khan, told Reuters: "We expect workers to allow the review process to proceed." He said that if protests broke out later in the day and owners were forced to shut factories, "we will have no option but to invoke the 'no work, no pay' provision". Industry representatives were due to meet the home minister on Monday.

Babul Akhter, general secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Industrial Workers Federation and a workers' representative on the new wage board, told Reuters that Bangladesh has "among the lowest garment wages in the world", and that owners who could not pay properly should negotiate better prices with international buyers. Owners point to higher costs, energy uncertainty linked to the war in the Middle East, and slowing demand in export markets.

## Sunday's protests

On Sunday police in Mirpur used batons, tear gas, sound grenades and water cannon against workers blocking the Mirpur-10 roundabout, The Business Standard (TBS) and bdnews24 reported. Protesters set fire to a police vehicle under the Mirpur-11 metro station at about 12.30 pm, Prothom Alo reported, and three metro stations were closed for about two hours.

The deputy commissioner of police for Mirpur, Hassan Mohammad Naser Rikabdar, told TBS at 8 pm that 19 people had been detained and legal action was being taken. Prothom Alo, citing police, put the number at 20, nine of them in Gazipur and 11 in Mirpur.

A deputy commissioner of the Detective Branch, Mohammad Rakib Khan, alleged that those detained in Mirpur were activists of the banned Awami League and its affiliates who had come from several districts to "sabotage" the labour movement, TBS reported. The Awami League's response to the allegation had not been reported, and no evidence was made public.

At least 20 people, including four or five police officers, were injured in the Mirpur clashes, Bangladesh Post reported. No deaths had been reported by Monday night.

## The wage board

The labour ministry formed a six-member minimum wage board for the garment sector on Sunday morning, headed by a senior district and sessions judge, Sheikh Ashfaqur Rahman. It includes two owners' representatives (from the BGMEA and the Bangladesh Employers' Federation), two workers' representatives, including the BNP-aligned Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal's president, and a Dhaka University professor as the independent member, according to Prothom Alo and TBS. No deadline for its recommendations has been reported.

Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk 30,000. The current minimum is Tk 12,500, Al Jazeera reported. Labour leaders told TBS the government had delayed forming the board for nearly two months.

## Orders at risk

The Dhaka University economist Selim Raihan told Reuters further unrest was possible and suggested raising wages in phases rather than in one large step. The current minimum was set in December 2023, and a review of the wage structure is due in December 2026, Business Standard reported.

## Background

Garments earn more than 80% of Bangladesh's export income, about $38.7 billion in the year to June 2026, and employ about four million people, TBS reported. Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China.

The protests began last week in Mirpur and spread to Gazipur, Ashulia and Savar. The government deployed Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) in Gazipur's industrial areas on Sunday; the force says it will stay until 7 November. Workers point to rising prices and a recent pay rise for government employees; owners say orders have weakened and costs have risen.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

India's apparel exporters compete with Bangladesh for orders from the same global brands, and buyers worried about delays may look elsewhere in the region. Bangladesh also buys cotton, yarn and fabric from India, much of it by road through West Bengal's Petrapole-Benapole crossing, so a long shutdown would hit traders and transporters on the Indian side.

Stability in Dhaka also matters for India-Bangladesh relations. Officials of the two countries are due to meet in Dhaka on 17 and 18 November, when Bangladesh says it will raise the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.

## What happens next

- Owners say they will invoke "no work, no pay", or close factories under Section 13(1) of the Labour Act, if unrest forces new shutdowns.
- The new wage board has not yet announced its first meeting.
- BGB personnel stay in Gazipur's industrial areas until 7 November.

## Key numbers

- 529: factories that halted production on Sunday (BGMEA sources, via TBS)
- 264: factories shut in Ashulia and Savar on Monday (The Daily Star)
- 20+: injured in Sunday's Mirpur clashes, including 4-5 police (Bangladesh Post)
- 10 lakh+: workers at those factories (TBS)
- Tk 30,000: the minimum monthly wage workers want
- Tk 12,500: the current minimum (Al Jazeera)
- 19-20: people detained on Sunday (police, via TBS and Prothom Alo)
